spatial_claims.claim: Two similar cones have circular bases on diameters ABCD and EFGH with axes (heights) KL and MN respectively, and similarity gives ABCD : EFGH :: KL : MN
An intermediate cone is constructed with the same base as the first cone (circle on diameter ABCD) and height equal to MN (the height of the second cone)
The intermediate cone and the second cone share the same height MN
The first cone (base ABCD, height KL) and the intermediate cone (base ABCD, height MN) share the same base (circle on diameter ABCD)
Cones on equal bases are to one another as their heights, justified via 12.10 (cone = 1/3 cylinder) and reasoning about cylinders
Each cone is one-third of the corresponding cylinder with the same base and height (by 12.10)

configuration_map: Three solids are constructed: (1) First cone with base = circle on diameter ABCD and height = KL; (2) Second cone with base = circle on diameter EFGH and height = MN; (3) Intermediate cone with base = circle on diameter ABCD and height = MN. The intermediate cone serves as a bridge, sharing its base with the first cone and its height with the second cone. This allows the ratio First:Second to be decomposed into (First:Intermediate) x (Intermediate:Second), where the first factor uses the shared base and the second factor uses the shared height. All three solids are well-defined cones with circular bases and finite heights. No points are placed inside or outside any figure, no angle decompositions occur, and no betweenness or ray-ordering claims are made.
pass_reason: The proof is primarily proportional/algebraic in nature. The only spatial constructions are three cones (first, second, intermediate) whose configurations are mutually consistent: two cones can share a base with different heights, and two cones can share a height with different bases. No angle decompositions, inside/outside claims, ray orderings, or other subtle spatial assumptions appear. The different approach from Heath (direct proportion vs. exhaustion) introduces no spatial contradictions.
